subject: radiology
title: Dawson Fingers, Multiple Sclerosis MRI and Dural Tail Sign

steps.title: Dawson fingers point from ventricles
steps.tx: **Dawson fingers** are ovoid multiple sclerosis plaques stretched along medullary veins, pointing radially away from the lateral ventricles like fingers on sagittal FLAIR images. The pictured sclerosis set shows the periventricular and callosal pattern that separates demyelination from the round, randomly angled white spots of small vessel disease. Plaques also favour the corpus callosum undersurface, juxtacortical U fibres, posterior fossa and cord, the four territories dissemination in space is counted from.

steps.title: Callosal and juxtacortical clues
steps.tx: **Callososeptal interface** plaques line the undersurface of the corpus callosum as small dots and dashes, a surface small vessel disease spares because its lesions avoid the callosum. Juxtacortical plaques touch cortex and bend U fibres, which ischaemic spots also spare by staying deep. Those two spared surfaces are the fastest discriminator on a crowded white matter scan in a young adult with transient neurological symptoms.

steps.title: Dissemination in space and time
steps.tx: **Dissemination in space** needs lesions in at least two of four territories: periventricular, cortical or juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord. Dissemination in time is proven by one enhancing and one non enhancing lesion together, or a new lesion on follow up, or oligoclonal bands standing in for time in current criteria. One good MRI with contrast therefore can complete a diagnosis that once waited for a second clinical attack.

steps.title: Active plaques enhance briefly
steps.tx: **Gadolinium enhancement** marks a plaque for roughly two to six weeks while its blood brain barrier leaks, then fades even though the T2 scar stays forever. Counting enhancing versus silent plaques on one scan stages disease activity and predicts near term relapses. Black holes, chronic T1 dark plaques, mark destroyed axons and accumulate with disability, so T1 burden quietly grades the destructive side of the disease.

steps.title: Cord lesions are short and peripheral
steps.tx: **Spinal cord plaques** in sclerosis run short, under two vertebral segments, sit peripherally in lateral and posterior columns and occupy part of the cord cross section. Longitudinally extensive lesions spanning three or more segments instead point to neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, which also attacks the optic nerves severely and carries aquaporin 4 antibodies. That length rule on one sagittal image reroutes the entire antibody and treatment pathway.

steps.title: Dural tail belongs to meningioma
steps.tx: **Dural tail sign** is a tapering rim of enhancing dura trailing from a dural based mass, the meningioma signature on post contrast MRI. The tail is reactive dura and tumour nests together, so surgeons resect it with the mass. Meningiomas also calcify, expand the diploic space with hyperostosis in the overlying skull and sit in parasagittal, convexity and sphenoid wing sites, often found incidentally in older women.

steps.title: Extra axial versus intra axial
steps.tx: **Extra axial signs** place a mass outside brain: a cerebrospinal fluid cleft between mass and cortex, displaced pial vessels, a broad dural base and buckled white matter pushed inward. Intra axial tumours instead expand cortex, lack a fluid cleft and infiltrate white matter tracts. That single compartment call halves the differential before enhancement pattern is even judged, meningioma and schwannoma outside, glioma and metastasis inside.

steps.title: Optic neuritis and the first scan
steps.tx: **Optic neuritis** inflames the optic nerve with pain on eye movement and central vision loss, and the same MRI that shows the swollen enhancing nerve surveys the brain for silent plaques. A normal brain MRI after optic neuritis carries a far lower later sclerosis risk than one already carrying periventricular lesions. Reporting both nerve and brain burden in the first study sets counselling, follow up rhythm and early disease modifying therapy discussions.
